summary:
Memento Mori is a spacecraft-inspired astronaut health-monitoring demonstration. We developed a web dashboard, backend API, and deterministic simulator that generate and display health telemetry for three synthetic crew members, along with equipment status, alerts, mission operations, and vehicle radiation readings.

The project addresses the challenge of making complex mission data easier to monitor and act on. When a simulated vital becomes abnormal, the dashboard highlights it and provides an alert review workflow. Operators can acknowledge the alert and apply a simulated precaution, after which the affected readings return toward baseline. Vehicle radiation data is presented separately from personal crew health data.

This project is important because clear, repeatable demonstrations can help teams explore how monitoring interfaces support timely awareness and response. It is an educational prototype, not a clinically validated system or official NASA product.
details:
Project overview

Memento Mori is a spacecraft-inspired astronaut health-monitoring demonstration. It combines a web dashboard with a backend API and a deterministic simulator that generates telemetry for three synthetic crew members. The dashboard shows simulated vital signs and trends, equipment status, alerts, radiation sensor readings for the vehicle, and mission operations.

When a simulated vital crosses an alert threshold, the app highlights the affected vital and presents an alert for review. In the demo, an operator can acknowledge the alert and apply a simulated precaution. That clears the associated simulated fault so subsequent readings can return toward the crew member’s baseline. The radiation measurements describe the vehicle environment and are kept separate from personal crew data.

Benefits and intended impact

The project brings several kinds of mission data into one interface, making it easier to demonstrate how operators might notice a change, review the relevant readings, and follow a response workflow. Its deterministic simulation makes scenarios repeatable for presentations and development, rather than relying on unpredictable data changes.

The intended impact is educational and exploratory: to make astronaut health-monitoring concepts and potential interface workflows easier to understand. It is a project demonstration, not a clinically validated system or an official NASA product.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML, and CSS.
  • Backend: Python with FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy, and SQLite.
  • Simulation: Rust for deterministic synthetic telemetry.
  • Hosting: Docker Compose and Caddy on an Ubuntu server.
  • Development and verification: Git, automated tests, linting, type checks, and production builds.

What makes it creative

The project combines a mission-control visual style with interactive, repeatable scenarios. It connects an alert to the affected vital, offers a demo-only recovery action, and lets viewers follow the simulated readings as they respond. It also distinguishes shared spacecraft radiation data from personal crew measurements, making the data model visible in the interface.

Factors considered

The design accounts for clear alert prioritization, understandable sensor status, repeatable data, and a responsive interface. It also considers accessibility preferences such as reduced motion, and separates simulated operator controls from the private worker endpoints used by the backend simulator. The most important limitation is that the thresholds and responses are for demonstration; they should not be treated as real medical guidance.
